Licentious

ly-SEN-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Licentious is disregarding accepted moral or sexual rules; unrestrained in conduct.

The pamphlet condemned the licentious parties held nightly at the estate on the edge of town.

Worked Example

The court gossiped for years about the duke's licentious behavior, one scandal after another following him from city to city.

Years of scandal following someone from city to city is exactly licentious behavior.

How Licentious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dissolute

dissolute: lacking moral restraint, especially in indulgence

promiscuous

promiscuous: having many casual sexual relationships

Antonyms

chaste

chaste: morally restrained, especially sexually

How Strong Is It? — permissive → depraved → licentious

permissive vs. licentious

permissive vs. licentious: Permissive describes ordinary leniency or a relaxed attitude toward rules, a mild and often harmless word; licentious describes a much more scandalous, sustained disregard for moral rules.

depraved vs. licentious

depraved vs. licentious: Depraved (taught earlier in this course) implies a deeper moral corruption or wickedness, while licentious is narrower, focused specifically on unrestrained sexual or social conduct.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — licent

root — licent: to be permitted (Latin (licere))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Licentious comes from Latin licere ('to be permitted') + -ious -- literally 'taking too much permission,' or behaving as if everything were allowed.

Use the root in a new word: license

Use the root in a new word: license: The same licere root gives us the everyday word license, official permission to do something -- licentious describes someone who grants themselves far more 'license' than is proper.

Licentious most often describes sustained, scandalous disregard for moral or sexual conventions, whether in a historical court, a work of fiction, or a modern news story.
